inputs.document:
A compiler is a program that translates source code written in one language
into another, usually a lower-level one. Classical designs separate a front end
(lexing, parsing, semantic analysis) from a back end (code generation), joined
by an intermediate representation. The separation lets one language target many
machines: adding a platform means writing a back end, not rewriting the
language. It also moves whole classes of error from run time to build time,
because the front end can reject a program that does not type-check. The
intermediate representation is the pivot point of the whole design.

# Compiler Design: Executive Brief

## What it is

A compiler translates source written for people into a form a machine can execute. The work splits into a *front end* that understands the language and a *back end* that targets a machine.

## Why the split matters

- **One front end, many targets.** Adding a platform means adding a back end, not rewriting the language.
- **Errors move earlier.** Type and scope mistakes surface at build time rather than in production.
- **The middle is reusable.** An intermediate representation lets analysis and optimisation be written once.

## What to take away

The intermediate representation is the load-bearing decision. Get it right and targets are cheap to add; get it wrong and every back end pays for it forever.
